builds.title: NoodleLab v2
builds.summary: A modular LED light instrument that turned into a distributed system.
builds.body:
A modular LED light instrument that turned into a distributed system. It started
as one microcontroller driving a few panels — but when it ran out of pins, I gave
every panel its own chip and linked them wirelessly. Now I can keep adding
surfaces without ever hitting a hardware wall, and they all animate together in
real time.

## How it works

An **ESP32-S3 core** (Adafruit FeatherS3) commands a fleet of **ESP-NOW
satellites** — 8×8, 16×16, and 12×8 matrices, an RGBW bar, a mic satellite, a
haptic dial remote, and a motorized disco ball — each its own ESP32-C3. The core
broadcasts one **58-byte packet**; every satellite receives the same packet and
renders locally, staying frame-synced without the core pushing every pixel.

- **Dual-core FreeRTOS** — radio on one core, FastLED render on the other, so they
  never step on each other (the S3's RMT peripheral fights the WiFi radio if you
  get the startup order wrong).
- **16 FastLED effects**, audio-reactive via a **512-point FFT** on the mic
  satellite that broadcasts bass/mid/treble/beat to the whole fleet.
- **Control surface:** three NeoPixel encoders, a NeoSlider, a ToF proximity
  sensor, capacitive touch, PCA9685-driven LED filaments + skull, and a
  lightning-bolt lane.

## Why it's built this way

The distributed architecture wasn't a flourish — it was running out of GPIO and
refusing to stop adding panels. Moving each surface to its own wireless board
means the system scales by adding *boards*, not pins.

entries.title: Mondrian, take two

media.caption: One layout at five settings of the Color knob (render)

entries.body: Reworked the motion. It used to slide one section out and back like a tray, and sometimes nothing actually changed. Now every line moves at once while part of the grid rebuilds and a color block slides to a new cell. That turned up a bug where remixing the whole canvas skipped moving the lines at all. The Color knob is now one smooth sweep built on the spacing of Mondrian's own red, blue and yellow, with his palette in the middle. Flashed it to the rig and the colors were off until I noticed the palette tint was still switched on.

entries.title: A Mondrian pattern for the Patternflow bank

media.caption: Three compositions from one run (render)

entries.body: Wrote my first pattern from scratch for the Patternflow bank: a Mondrian grid that keeps rearranging itself. It builds the layout by splitting the canvas in two and then splitting the pieces, which is how his paintings are put together, so it's always a valid composition. Built a small browser harness to work on it in JavaScript first, then hand-ported it to C++ for the hub75. The two versions match pixel for pixel.

entries.title: Landscape TFT + chrome refresh; the Patternflow bank
entries.body: Recomposed the entire UI for a landscape 320×240 ST7789 mount — one-row header, framed menus, Live Control and Chladni re-laid-out. Landed the Patternflow bank too: hand-ported JS shader-style patterns running on all three boards, with the red Qwiic button as a palette dice.

entries.title: 21 effects, a palette system, and 'Noodle 2K'
entries.body: Big content wave: a trimmed 2D particle engine and the WLED particle effects (catalog to 21), a real 16-band GEQ spectrum analyzer, and a global palette system with host-parity tests and a dial palette picker. Rebranded the whole thing "Noodle 2K" with a new layered power-on intro. Also brought up a hub75 MatrixPortal satellite doing native 64×32.

entries.title: The big rebuild — bare MCU, Chladni, cyberpunk chrome
entries.body: Stripped the rig back to a bare MCU and brought it up clean: retired the icon and (later) 8×12 sats, drove the 16×16 locally, moved SparkFun inputs to their own I2C bus, and replaced the wireframe screensaver with a live Chladni-plate visualizer. Also redid the whole UI on an anti-aliased "chrome" kit and killed the flicker.

entries.title: Portability pass + matrix sat moves to an S3
entries.body: Made the whole project portable to a new machine — pinned the pioarduino platform by URL across every board so builds are reproducible. Ported the 12×8 matrix satellite to a dual-core ESP32-S3 SuperMini for a better radio, and added a baked Pac-Chase animation source for the 16×16.

entries.title: Disco-ball satellite — and a nasty ground-noise lesson

media.caption: Printed skull over the spinning disco ball

entries.body: Added a motorized disco ball as its own satellite (stepper + spot LED + OLED) with a dedicated LiveTarget. First version ran the stepper off main power and it made the ground filthy — the noise bled into the rest of the Noodle. Its own supply fixed it. Classic motor-on-shared-ground trap.

entries.title: ESP-NOW only, plus a screen-capture path

media.caption: Lit desk with the pixel matrix running

entries.body: Dropped WiFi association entirely — the Console runs pure ESP-NOW now. Started the screen-share path (browser → ingest → matrix) and a LittleFS clip store, so I can push real captured pixels to the 16×16, not just generated effects.

entries.title: Dial remote, sprite overlays, playlists

media.caption: Hex panels and RGB orb on the bench

entries.body: Added the dial sat as a wireless remote with a live preview canvas, a composite overlay source (16×16 pattern + centered 8×8 icon), Qwiic forward/back buttons for the pattern stack, and curated playlists. Also cut the dead DDP path entirely.

entries.title: The fleet takes shape — bar, 8×8, 16×16 satellites
entries.body: Built out the pixel satellites — a 1×30 bar, an 8×8 icon panel, a 16×16 matrix — each its own board rendering locally off a shared wire format (v5). The GPIO wall is officially gone; I scale by adding boards now.

entries.title: Audio satellite — first ESP-NOW peer, beat detection
entries.body: First satellite: a separate board with a mic running spectral-flux, bass-leaning beat detection, broadcasting audio features over peered ESP-NOW so every effect can react in lockstep. This is where it stopped being one board.

entries.title: Three encoders, per-target ownership, Source Map
entries.body: Wired up three NeoPixel rotary encoders with per-target slot ownership (highest I2C address = slot 0), a Source Map for per-surface assignment, and retired Pixelblaze in favor of the native engine. The control surface is starting to feel like a real instrument panel.

entries.title: Descriptor-table effect engine + the FeatherWing

media.caption: The full instrument lit

entries.body: Stood up the real effects engine — a descriptor table, 10 effects to start — plus a 4×8 NeoPixel FeatherWing mirroring the matrix and a TPS61169 gamma-corrected filament driver. The whole surface is lit and animating together now.

entries.title: Ran out of pins — going distributed
entries.body: Added an external 8×8 and hit the GPIO wall. That's the decision point: every LED surface becomes its own ESP-NOW satellite, so the system scales by adding boards, not pins. Everything after this is that idea playing out.

entries.title: Filaments breathing, fiber optics, live Pixelblaze

media.caption: Driver board lighting fiber-optic strands

entries.body: PCA9685 LED filaments on a sine-breath offset, a Pixelblaze websocket path for browsing and streaming patterns live, and the patterns/ scaffolding. First time the thing looked less like a prototype and more like an instrument.

entries.title: Dual-core FreeRTOS — network off the render path
entries.body: Decomposed the firmware into four FreeRTOS tasks across both cores, moving the network onto Core 0 so the radio and the LED render stop fighting each other. This is the backbone everything else hangs off.

entries.title: Noodle 2.0 — core up and running in a day
entries.body: Rebuilt from the breadboard onto a FeatherS3. In one sitting: display + encoder + buttons working, a sensor dashboard (distance, light, NeoPixel), WLED control, and a direct 4×12 matrix with an 8×8 icon slideshow. The solid STEMMA-QT prototyping paid off immediately.

entries.title: Noodle 1 — the breadboard prototype that didn't scale
entries.body:
First pass at the idea: one controller driving a series of LED grids and
filaments. Built it on a breadboard with a rat's nest of wires. It worked, barely,
but it was obvious this would never scale — every new surface meant more jumpers
and more flakiness. Tore it down and went looking for a more solid way to
prototype (landed on Adafruit STEMMA QT modules).

builds.title: kFun
builds.summary: Two handheld game consoles built from one codebase.
builds.body:
Two handheld consoles, one codebase. **tinyfun** is a LOLIN S3 Mini Pro with a
128×128 screen and three buttons; **bigfun** is an ESP32-S3 SuperMini with a
320×240 screen and six. A single `KFUN_WIDE` compile-time split is all that
separates them — pins live only in each board's `Config.h`, and nothing in the
engine, UI, or games ever names a GPIO. Some slots are literally a different
game per console: Invaders becomes Galaga on the wide board, Breakout becomes
Arkanoid.

The engine is a non-blocking Game contract (`init` / `update(dt)` / `render`)
running at a fixed 60 Hz, with every game placement-new'd into a single 12 KB
arena that fails to compile if it won't fit. The framebuffer is pinned to SRAM
because PSRAM faults on per-pixel writes, and the quit chord is un-swallowable so
a misbehaving game can never trap you. Highlights among the six slots: **SkyGrid**,
an original software 3D renderer with no z-buffer that pushes 128 triangles at
60 fps, and **Backgammon**, a fully rules-checked, natively unit-tested engine
that plays 2-ply expectimax on bigfun with doubling cube, Crawford, and NVS match
save.

Enrolled a third-batch tinyfun board (MAC 28:84:85:67:b1:44) as panel profile B.
Each batch of panels drifts a little, so a new profile beats fighting the same

entries.title: Shake to restart, and a printable case
entries.body:
Wired up a QMI8658C shake HAL — a physical shake restarts the current game — with a
no-op stub on bigfun since it has no IMU, and made the engine resume games from NVS
so you pick up where you left off. Also packaged the enclosure as a sliceable 3MF
project so the shell is one print away.

entries.title: megafun folds in, three boards
entries.body:
Folded megafun into the monorepo so all three boards share one core, gated by
capability flags instead of forks. Added per-board panel profiles with an on-board
tuner and enrolled the original tinyfun board as profile M1, gave the launcher an
attract auto-rotate after idle, and rewrote the README for three boards with a
pre-commit guardrail to keep it honest.

entries.title: Backgammon VS PLAYER over ESP-NOW
entries.body:
Added a VS PLAYER mode to Backgammon over an ESP-NOW link, built up phase by phase —
turn transport first, then game-over sync, then the doubling cube — mirroring the
megafun implementation. Followed it with a per-device mirror and a resilience layer
so a dropped packet doesn't desync the board, keeping mega and bigfun at parity.

entries.title: Galaga trains and SkyGrid forks
entries.body:
Deepened the wide-board games: Galaga got enemy trains and a difficulty ladder,
SkyGrid got track forks and proper ship motion, and both got a round of UI effects
that use the extra screen real estate the wide board offers.

Galaga takes over the Invaders slot on bigfun with auto-fire, so the wide board and

entries.title: PSRAM enabled, Backgammon Hard AI goes 2-ply expectimax
entries.body:
Enabled the board's 2MB PSRAM on bigfun. Reworked the Backgammon Hard AI to run
2-ply expectimax, so it evaluates the dice one roll deep rather than grabbing the
nearest legal move.

entries.title: Particle effects across both boards, and real Backgammon match play
entries.body:
Added particle and shake effects across both consoles: kill and death pops in
Invaders, line-clear debris in Tetris, checker slide-and-capture pops in Backgammon,
glide on Snake, and brick-break and life-loss shakes in Breakout. Also stood up real
match play in bigfun Backgammon — 5-point match, doubling cube, difficulty, NVS save
— and gave the intro a Slackey wordmark with glow and particles.

entries.title: Merged into the kFun monorepo, shared console on the SuperMini

media.caption: bigfun next to the smaller tinyfun

entries.body:
Restructured everything into the kFun monorepo — a shared common/ with tinyfun/ and
bigfun/ on top — and got the full app booting the shared console on the SuperMini.
Then a round of art and effects work on the wide board: landscape backgammon with
traditional triangle points, a centred Tetris well with side panels, an Arkanoid
rebuild, a sprite pipeline off the Kenney CC0 art, launcher attract cards, nebula
backgrounds with post-FX, and a themed game-over screen.

entries.title: Backgammon replaces Asteroids, Canyon renamed to SkyGrid
entries.body:
Swapped Asteroids out for Backgammon and renamed Canyon to SkyGrid, and added a help
screen listing the button controls. Redrew the board, made a piece's second move
findable, added bear-off auto and bigger dice. Also cut the Slackey case logo SVGs
for the eventual printed shell.

entries.title: First TinyFun boot on the S3 Mini Pro
entries.body:
First working console: a five-game handheld on the LOLIN S3 Mini Pro driving a
128×128 panel. Brought up the boot screen and a custom typeface, and got CANYON — a
3D anti-gravity racer — running on the panel. Also did an Asteroids pass: added a
3-shot spread and lightened the opening wave so the first screen isn't a full field
of rocks.

builds.title: vizBot
builds.summary: A companion robot with a face, personalities, and a cloud backend.
builds.body:
vizBot is a little companion robot with a face — 25 procedurally-drawn
expressions and a handful of personalities that decide how it reacts to the
room. It started as an LED matrix controller and grew a face, then a voice, then
opinions. Everything on the screen is drawn from primitives (eyes, mouths, tweened
transitions), so the same face engine renders identically across a Waveshare LCD,
an M5 Core S3, and a 1-bit 128×64 OLED. It listens with a 512-point FFT on the
Core S3 mic and reacts to sound, gets audio-reactive ambient effects, drives a
**StackChan** servo base for physical head movement, and pushes its speech out to
a **WLED matrix over DDP** — direct pixel control, no scroll-effect games.

Under the hood it's dual-core FreeRTOS: rendering on one core, WiFi/HTTP/mesh and
an isolated cloud task on the other. The bots talk to **vizCloud** — a separate
Node.js backend I run on DigitalOcean — to register, sync telemetry, join fleet
groups, and pull server-queued commands, including NTP-scheduled commands so a
whole room of bots can move together. On the local side they form an **ESP-NOW
mesh** that does cooperative WLED arbitration: two bots won't stomp the same
matrix, and one will even defer its speech bubble until a peer releases the
display. Four of them are living in other places now — a real fleet in the wild.

entries.title: StackChan servo hardening + fleet deployment
entries.body: Chased the StackChan head stalls to ground: calibrated the pitch zero, moved to the M5 StackChan-BSP driver, armed the servos properly with position mode and torque, and replaced a flaky servo watchdog with a blind 5-minute rail cycle plus a graceful glide back to pose after reinit instead of snapping home. Four vizBots are now running in other locations, and vizCloud is live for adding content.

entries.title: vizMini — the face on an ESP32-C3 and an OLED
entries.body: Spun off vizMini: a standalone, pared-down vizbot for an ESP32-C3 SuperMini driving a 1-bit 128×64 OLED — the same face engine on the cheapest hardware it would run on. Added an onboard NeoPixel rainbow glow, swapped the capacitive pad for a debounced pushbutton, dropped the sleep state so it stays awake, and added web OTA updates.

entries.title: Neon-green build photos + cold-boot servo fix

media.caption: The neon-green vizBot with its OLED face

entries.body: The bot in the flesh — neon-green shell, OLED face, StackChan base underneath. Fixed the StackChan servos refusing to answer through a cold-boot start-up by retrying the servo ping until they woke. Kept web control responsive by decoupling it from the cloud sync, and fixed a registration truncation bug that was cutting device names short.

entries.title: Audio-reactive ambient effects + kaleidoscope pass
entries.body: Made all 16 ambient effects audio-reactive — first the ambient set and a base-LED audio mode, then mappings for the remaining 12, then a punch-up on Plasma/Galaxy/Stripes/Puzzle with a base-LED audio overlay. Added a kaleidoscope post-processing pass on top of the ambient effects and a drama slider to dial the intensity.

entries.title: vizBot 3.0 — StackChan body target
entries.body: vizBot 3.0 put the face on a StackChan body. Built up in phases: a minimum-viable StackChan build target, StackChan hardware driver bring-up, web endpoints with pitch safety clamping, then servo expressivity, touch reactions, idle sweeps, and a chill mode. Replaced the old ambient effects with 16 patterns ported from noodle-v2. Had to pin M5GFX@0.2.19 — 0.2.21 gave the Core S3 a black screen.

entries.title: PlatformIO migration + a SAM2695 MIDI synth
entries.body: Moved vizbot and vizpow off the Arduino IDE onto PlatformIO for reproducible builds and versioned firmware binaries, with bins published to a top-level builds/ directory. Integrated a SAM2695 MIDI synthesizer across several phases, including cloud MIDI sequence caching and sync so the bot can pull tunes down. It plays MIDI now in addition to speech.

entries.title: vizCloud, multi-bot orchestration, and an ESP-NOW mesh
entries.body: Landed vizCloud integration with a static BSS framebuffer for zero-flicker TLS, an isolated cloud task on Core 0, and a unified WiFi task. Built Stage 4/5 multi-bot orchestration on top of it. Added an ESP-NOW local mesh doing cooperative WLED arbitration — flag bits in a broadcast packet so two bots won't drive the same matrix at once, with one deferring its speech bubble until a peer releases the display.

entries.title: Senses — mic, proximity, light, and a hologram mode
entries.body: Added sensor input: a mic audio-analysis driver, a proximity + ambient-light sensor driver, sound-reactive and proximity-reactive expressions, and auto-brightness. Reworked the face with 6 eye shapes, 6 mouth shapes, and 8 new expressions, and redid the speech bubble with a proportional font that positions off the sensors. Added a hologram mode — a horizontal LCD mirror for a Pepper's-ghost prism.

entries.title: LovyanGFX migration + a tween system
entries.body: Migrated the LCD target from Arduino_GFX to LovyanGFX; chased a blue tint and dim brightness afterward, and unified canvas management along the way. Built a tween system with 8 easing functions and wired it into the main loop, replacing the hand-rolled smoothstep and linear lerps. Expression transitions and look-around animations now run on the easing curves.

entries.title: M5 Core S3 target + per-device identity
entries.body: Added an M5Stack Core S3 target with a multi-screen layout system: a layout.h that derives the UI from screen size, so a new display is a compile flag rather than a rewrite. Gave each bot its own identity — a unique per-device SSID and mDNS hostname derived from the eFuse MAC, plus a user-settable device name for a memorable hostname. Groundwork for running more than one bot at a time.

entries.title: WLED integration — from scroll effects to raw DDP
entries.body: Added forwarding of the bot's speech to a WLED LED matrix. First approach drove WLED's built-in scrolling text effect; fought it for days over scroll speed, trails, jump cuts, and effect reinit on consecutive words. Switched to direct pixel control over DDP, drawing the text myself, which gave immediate clean frames without relying on the effect engine.

entries.title: Networking hardening and the Core 0 crash
entries.body: Spent several days hardening the networking. Added a sequential boot loader with onscreen diagnostics, an I2C mutex and command queue for race safety, moved the web server to a FreeRTOS task on Core 0, added WiFi provisioning with NVS-stored credentials, and a captive portal with DNS + mDNS auto-redirect. The Core 0 crash took the longest — chased it through watchdog reconfigures and stack-size bumps before the WiFi task stayed up. Closed out with persistent settings and a health heartbeat.

entries.title: Face engine and the split into vizBot
entries.body: Built the face engine in phases: core face with 12 expressions, then sayings and speech bubbles, then personality presets and a full web UI, then 20 expressions with backgrounds. Everything is drawn from primitives so it scales with the screen. Split the firmware in two — vizpow keeps the effects, vizbot gets the face — and renamed the WiFi AP from VizPow to vizBot.

entries.title: Hi-res LCD, an ESP8266 port, and the vizPow name
entries.body: Brought up a hi-res LCD rendering mode with a touch menu so the effects render on a real screen, not just a matrix. Ported the engine to an ESP8266 LED matrix target to test how portable it was. Renamed the project to vizPow. Same core engine, more display surfaces.

entries.title: Emoji mode, icon sprites, and shake-to-switch
entries.body: Added an emoji display mode with a sprite picker and 32 icon sprites, plus icon tooling to manage them. Wired up a shuffle-bag auto-cycle for effects and palettes so they don't repeat too soon. Added a shake gesture read off the IMU to change modes.

entries.title: Bring-up — ESP32-S3 LED matrix controller
entries.body: Started the project as a plain ESP32-S3 LED matrix controller. Sorted the build config, laid out the folder structure, and pushed pixels to the grid. Scope at this point is a board, a matrix, and a controller that renders effects — no face, no cloud, no gestures yet.

builds.title: ESP32 Plane Radar
builds.summary: A desktop ADS-B aircraft scope on a round LCD.
builds.body:
A desktop ADS-B aircraft **radar scope**. It paints the live traffic around my
home lat/lon onto a green sonar grid — a rotating sweep with a comet trail,
heading triangles with speed vectors out front, callsign/type/altitude tags, and
anything out of range parked as a bearing-dot on the rim. The data comes from the
public **adsb.fi opendata REST API** over HTTPS (no local receiver), polled every
3 seconds for up to **64 aircraft**, with the radius scaled to the screen edge.
It all lives on a **GC9A01 1.28" round LCD** (240×240, LovyanGFX) driven by an
**ESP32-C3 Super Mini**, in a printed slatted case with a BOOT button and an
optional touch pad to cycle range.

## How it's built

The whole thing is **heap-aware everywhere**, because TLS eats RAM. I render into
an **8-bit off-screen sprite framebuffer** (chosen specifically to survive the
heap pressure of a live HTTPS poll), stream-parse the JSON with a field filter so
I never hold the whole body, and check the heap *before* opening the socket. Between
polls the scope **dead-reckons each plane forward** from its last heading and speed
so motion stays smooth at 30 fps — capped, so a dropped poll or an outage can't
fling a target off the edge. There's also a full **gzipped SPA companion app baked
into flash** — radar, flight list, stats, and detail cards served off `/api/flights`,
with the browser enriching routes and photos from adsbdb and planespotters. An
**ESP32-S3 target** exists too, for the better radio.

entries.title: Empty radar bug: de-chunk the ADS-B body
entries.body: Radar had started coming up empty — grid, sweep, no planes. Turned out the ADS-B endpoint was returning its response with **chunked transfer encoding**, and my stream parser was choking on the chunk-size markers instead of the JSON. De-chunked the body before parsing and the traffic came right back. Sneaky one: the fetch succeeded, the heap was fine, it was just quietly feeding garbage to the parser.

entries.title: Map underlay + multi-leg routes
entries.body:
Added a faint **map underlay** to both scopes — coast, lakes, rivers, roads — drawn dim enough to give a sense of place without fighting the traffic on top. It makes the whole thing legible: you can tell a plane is following a river valley or lined up on a road.

Also taught the route display to handle **multi-leg trips**: it now shows every stop on the route and highlights the leg the aircraft is currently flying, instead of collapsing everything to origin-and-destination. (Refreshed the README a couple of days earlier while I was in here.)

entries.title: The web companion app — touch radar in the browser
entries.body:
Big day for the browser side. Built an **interactive touch radar web UI** served straight off the device, with per-device themes and — the important part — a **heap fix** so serving the SPA doesn't collide with the live ADS-B poll. The app is gzipped and baked into flash; it hits `/api/flights` for the traffic and lets the browser enrich each plane with route and photo data. Added a page header that shows live context so you know what you're looking at without hunting.

On the hardware side, **hardened the TTP223 range-touch input** against a flapping line — the capacitive pad was chattering and cycling range on its own, so I debounced it into behaving. Also swept the repo: stopped tracking `.DS_Store` junk and told git to ignore the capsule-radar reference project I'd been reading for ideas.

entries.title: Sweep goes under the grid
entries.body: Small layering fix that makes a big visual difference: render the radar sweep *beneath* the grid instead of over it. Now the sweep glow reads as light passing under the graticule, and the grid lines and plane markers stay crisp on top. Draw order is half the battle with these sprite composites.

entries.title: Onboard RGB status light + a scanning overlay
entries.body: Put the C3's onboard RGB LED to work as a status light with a little animation, and added a scanning overlay on top of the scope so it reads more like radar and less like a static plot. Also dropped the 100 km range option — at that zoom the projection distortion gets silly and I never actually use it. The useful ranges are the close ones.

entries.title: Forked a plane-radar project, then rebuilt it heap-first

media.caption: Round GC9A01 wired up on the bench
Close on the radar scope — sweep and callsigns
Display fitted into the printed slatted housing
The finished retro-cube radar, green sweep + traffic

entries.body:
Started from a modern-SDK fork of a plane-radar project on the ESP32-C3, then more or less gutted it. The stock build locked up periodically — it was firing a burst of ADS-B requests and buffering whole response bodies. Fixed that with a single request on a backoff and a **stream-parse** so I only ever pull the fields I need. That alone stopped the lockups.

From there it was a founding rebuild in one long session: a **dual-core split** with the network fetch on its own task so rendering never stalls, and **smooth plane interpolation** so targets glide between the 3-second polls instead of teleporting. Added an **ESP32-S3 Super Mini target** for the better radio, plus WiFi retry hardening so a flaky connect recovers instead of hanging. Then the bells and whistles: **16-bit color at 80 MHz SPI** on the S3, and the **radar sweep with a comet trail paced at 30 fps**. By the end it was a live scope — round LCD, green grid, real callsigns — sitting in the printed slatted cube on the desk.

builds.title: PhantasyFish
builds.body:
Fantasy sports for Phish setlists — you predict a show before the band plays, then
score on how close you got. I built and run the whole stack: the game itself, the
automated scoring engine, an AI that drafts setlists from history, leaderboards, and
the email that ties it together. It's been live and played for over a year.

Under the hood it's full-stack TypeScript — a React front end over Express and
PostgreSQL with Drizzle ORM. The **scoring engine** hands out song, set,
exact-position, opener–closer, and shared-bustout bonuses, and it fires
automatically the moment the official setlist posts. **WookBot** is an OpenAI setlist
generator built on historical play patterns, and around all of it sit leaderboards
(global / tour / show), research tools, an admin console, and transactional email.

## By the numbers (year one)

115 players across 6 tours and 28 venues · 74 shows scored · 1,155 predictions ·
65,054 points · 248 top score · **398 exact song positions nailed** · 2,501 songs
placed in the right set · 99 bustouts · 67 AI-generated setlists · a 959-song catalog.

entries.title: Year one, by the numbers
entries.body:
Did a full data run and totted up the first year: 115 players across 6 tours and 28 venues,
74 shows scored, 1,155 predictions, 65,054 points earned. Also in the totals: 398 exact
song positions nailed, 2,501 songs placed in the right set, 99 bustouts called, and 67
setlists generated by WookBot. A whole game, live and played, built and run start to finish
over the year.

entries.title: phish.net outage resilience: local mirror, DB fallback, manual scoring
entries.body:
Built resilience against the phish.net data source going down mid-show, the worst failure
mode for a live-scoring game. Added a local phish.net mirror with background sync, a
database fallback for show endpoints when the API is blocked, and the ability to score
straight from a hand-entered live setlist when the network won't cooperate. A bad night on
someone else's server no longer takes the game down with it.

entries.title: Import upcoming shows into a tour, modular admin routes
entries.body:
Added an admin feature to import upcoming shows straight into a tour, so setting up a new
season is a few clicks instead of hand-entering a schedule. This came after splitting the
admin routes out of one giant file into modular pieces — the console had grown enough that
the routing needed to be maintainable, not just working. The refactor keeps the cost of
adding the next feature down.

entries.title: Tour Wrapped recap page and personalized email links
entries.body:
Built a Tour Wrapped stats page: a per-player recap of the tour just played — your best
calls, your points, your rarities. Wired a personalized wrappedLink variable into the email
system so every player gets a direct link to their own recap, keyed to the right tour. It
took a few follow-up fixes to make the callout point at the correct completed tour, and
Wrapped turned out to be the thing people actually shared.

entries.title: Final summer-tour data pull, season closeout
entries.body:
Ran the last data pull for summer tour and let the season settle. The cycle for running
this: a burst of live scoring while shows are happening, then a quiet stretch to reconcile
data, fix what scored wrong, and get ready for the next run. First full tour season in the
books.

entries.title: Scores dashboard and a stats sidebar
entries.body:
Shipped a scores dashboard and a stats sidebar alongside the research tools: a song
explorer with a selector, tour-plays columns, and the numbers players use to reason about
what the band will open with. The research side is where the hardcore players build
predictions off gap data and tour history rather than guesses.

entries.title: Live mode: scoring as the show happens
entries.body:
Summer tour meant live mode: a live view that scores predictions in near real time as a
setlist comes in, with an admin side to drive it song by song. Added a compact setlist
display for the live page and pushed bustout callouts right into it, so the leaderboard
reshuffles as each song is entered while the band is still playing.

entries.title: Tour manager and per-tour song counts
entries.body:
Built a tour manager and started tracking per-tour song counts — how many times each song
has been played on the current run. Phish is organized by tour, so almost every view worth
having — leaderboards, research, Wrapped stats — depends on knowing which shows belong to
which tour. Getting that structure right unlocked a lot of the features that came after.

entries.title: Email manager 1.0
entries.body:
Stood up the transactional email system on Resend: a composer, refined templates, and a
logs viewer to see what actually went out. The old ad-hoc emailers are gone, replaced by
one manager driven from the admin side. A day later I added a rate limiter so a large send
can't get the domain flagged.

entries.title: Editing setlists by hand
entries.body:
Added an admin interface for editing setlist details directly, because the official data
isn't always right, or isn't posted yet, and the whole scoring run depends on it. Now a
mangled setlist can be corrected or an auto-generated one refined before it scores, with
better error handling for when the source data is malformed. The scoring run is only as
good as the setlist it's fed.

entries.title: Admin console 1.0
entries.body:
Built the back office: admin pages to manage files, songs, users, and WookBot setlists
from one place. Running a live game means constantly touching data — fixing a song entry,
checking an account, curating a generated setlist — and doing that directly against the
database was getting slow. The console replaced a batch of one-off scripts with actual
screens.

entries.title: Scoring engine: bustout detection from gap data, bonus breakdown
entries.body:
Reworked the scoring engine for fairness. Bustout detection now uses gap data — the stretch
of shows since a song was last played — so calling a rarity is worth real bonus points, and
shared bustouts pay out to everyone who called them. Tightened the exact-position accuracy
scoring, and started surfacing the bonus breakdown on the score page so players can see
exactly why they earned each point instead of trusting a single total.

entries.title: WookBot: OpenAI setlist generator goes public
entries.body:
WookBot went public: an OpenAI-backed generator that drafts a plausible setlist for an
upcoming show from historical play patterns. Gave it a home-page module showing the show
date and venue, a selector to browse past generations, and skeleton loading states during
generation. It only pulls from published show data, so the suggestions stay grounded in
songs the band actually plays.

entries.title: Leaderboards: global, tour, single-show
entries.body:
Added leaderboards with three scopes: a global board across all players, a per-tour board
scoped to the current run, and a single-show board for one show's predictions. Each board
ranks the top predictors for its scope, and each board's view buttons link straight to the
relevant scorecards, so you can go from a ranked name to that player's scored prediction in
one click. This is the piece that turns scored predictions into an ongoing competition
between shows.

entries.title: Random-fill button, setlist-save fixes, spam-folder reminder
entries.body:
Closing out the first playable week. Added a random-fill button that populates a setlist
with random songs, for people who want to jump in without building one by hand. Fixed a
batch of setlist-saving bugs that had been dropping songs. Added a check-your-spam-folder
reminder for the account verification email, since sign-ups were coming in and the
verification mail was landing in spam folders.

entries.title: Scorecards and the first scored show
entries.body:
Built the scorecard: a two-column set 1 / set 2 layout with a breakdown showing which
songs contributed to your points. Wired in real 2024 show data to score predictions
against, so a finished prediction could be scored for the first time. The score button
stays hidden until a show is officially scored, so players don't see a wall of zeros
before the band has played.

every load. Prediction saving landed the same day, so the core loop — build a setlist,
save it as a prediction — was working end to end from day one.

builds.title: StackLED
builds.summary: A handheld LED stacker arcade game.
builds.body:
It's the carnival Stacker — the skill-tester where you pile a sliding light bar
up a tower. A lit bar slides left and right across a tall 8×32 field; you mash
the button to drop it, and only the pixels that overlap the row below survive.
Overhang gets trimmed, so the bar gets narrower every time you're sloppy. Reach
the top to clear the level; each one runs faster and thinner than the last. Five
hand-authored levels, then it goes procedurally endless. Runs on an ESP32-C3
Super Mini driving four MAX7219 panels, with an illuminated button and a speaker
that can scream.

The twist I'm proudest of: the bar **is** your health meter. There's no separate
lives counter — the same bar you're stacking erodes on wall-bounces and misses,
and when its width hits zero, you're done. Under the hood the whole stack is pure
bitmask math: each row is a `uint8_t`, a new row AND'd with the one below is the
survivors, popcount is your width, count-trailing-zeros is the left edge. No
arrays of pixels, just bit twiddling and a non-blocking `millis()` state machine.
I built it at **makedown**, a crew maker-weekend where everyone hauls in their
own project — I brought a bag of panels and a green 3D-printed wand, and left
with a game.

builds.title: The Cyberdeck (noode-exp)
builds.summary: A portable Raspberry Pi workstation with a custom ESP32 electronics bench.
builds.body:
The Cyberdeck is a portable computer I built to be my bench, not just sit on it. At
its core is an 8 GB **Raspberry Pi 5** with a **7" touchscreen**, a **Mii Bluetooth
keyboard**, and an **M5Stack Stick / Joy-C** standing in as the mouse — all folded
into a custom-designed case with a matching box for the electronics side. There's no
Pi code here; the deck is a computer I assembled, and the repo name (`noodle-exp`)
belongs to the *other* half of the rig.

That other half is **noode-exp**, a standalone ESP32-S3 gadget that lives on the deck
as its electronics workbench. It's a Lonely Binary **ESP32-S3 N16R8** driving a 2"
**ST7789**, an EC11 encoder + KY-023 joystick, a **4×4 WS2812 matrix**, a pair of LED
filament "noodles" (the name), and an **HLK-LD2412 mmWave presence radar** — all under
~2500 lines of monolithic C++ with **11 modes** (Steer Cube, Cube Swarm, Warp Tunnel,
Box Physics, Chladni, Kaleido, Filaments, LED Matrix, Color Pick, Room Radar, Presence
Log). It's dual-core with a PSRAM framebuffer and no connectivity at all — a genuinely
standalone appliance. The v1 case geometry came out broken, so v2 got a redesigned
keyboard tray, which is the build hero.

*(A fuller, git-derived history is pending — this devlog is reconstructed from the
photos and technical notes because the repo export 404'd on a name typo.)*

The core is a non-blocking `millis()` state machine running pure bitmask stack logic. Each row is a `uint8_t`. To land a piece, AND a candidate row with the row below to keep only the overlapping pixels; popcount gives the resulting width, count-trailing-zeros gives the left edge. No pixel arrays — the whole field is bits. Renamed the project to STACKLED and removed a duplicate copy of the build guide. Wrote the build guide out in full, including 5-band resistor bodies drawn with the correct color codes so the BOM reads directly off the page. High score is stored in NVS, so it survives a power cycle.

recent.title: First Pi 5 build — 7\" touch, Bluetooth keyboard, Joy-C mouse
recent.body: Started assembling the deck around an 8 GB Raspberry Pi 5 with a 7" touchscreen as the main display. Text input comes from a Mii Bluetooth keyboard; pointer input from an M5Stack Stick running a Joy-C, which stands in as the mouse. Together they make the deck a self-contained portable computer with no external host. No Pi software yet — this half of the rig is hardware assembly only.

recent.title: vizMini — the face on an ESP32-C3 and an OLED
recent.body: Spun off vizMini: a standalone, pared-down vizbot for an ESP32-C3 SuperMini driving a 1-bit 128×64 OLED — the same face engine on the cheapest hardware it would run on. Added an onboard NeoPixel rainbow glow, swapped the capacitive pad for a debounced pushbutton, dropped the sleep state so it stays awake, and added web OTA updates.

recent.title: Neon-green build photos + cold-boot servo fix

One of the 25 procedurally-drawn expressions

recent.body: The bot in the flesh — neon-green shell, OLED face, StackChan base underneath. Fixed the StackChan servos refusing to answer through a cold-boot start-up by retrying the servo ping until they woke. Kept web control responsive by decoupling it from the cloud sync, and fixed a registration truncation bug that was cutting device names short.

recent.title: Sweep goes under the grid
recent.body: Small layering fix that makes a big visual difference: render the radar sweep *beneath* the grid instead of over it. Now the sweep glow reads as light passing under the graticule, and the grid lines and plane markers stay crisp on top. Draw order is half the battle with these sprite composites.

recent.title: Onboard RGB status light + a scanning overlay
recent.body: Put the C3's onboard RGB LED to work as a status light with a little animation, and added a scanning overlay on top of the scope so it reads more like radar and less like a static plot. Also dropped the 100 km range option — at that zoom the projection distortion gets silly and I never actually use it. The useful ranges are the close ones.

recent.title: Portability pass + matrix sat moves to an S3
recent.body: Made the whole project portable to a new machine — pinned the pioarduino platform by URL across every board so builds are reproducible. Ported the 12×8 matrix satellite to a dual-core ESP32-S3 SuperMini for a better radio, and added a baked Pac-Chase animation source for the 16×16.

recent.title: Forked a plane-radar project, then rebuilt it heap-first

media.caption: Round GC9A01 wired up on the bench
Close on the radar scope — sweep and callsigns
Display fitted into the printed slatted housing
The finished retro-cube radar, green sweep + traffic

recent.body:
Started from a modern-SDK fork of a plane-radar project on the ESP32-C3, then more or less gutted it. The stock build locked up periodically — it was firing a burst of ADS-B requests and buffering whole response bodies. Fixed that with a single request on a backoff and a **stream-parse** so I only ever pull the fields I need. That alone stopped the lockups.

From there it was a founding rebuild in one long session: a **dual-core split** with the network fetch on its own task so rendering never stalls, and **smooth plane interpolation** so targets glide between the 3-second polls instead of teleporting. Added an **ESP32-S3 Super Mini target** for the better radio, plus WiFi retry hardening so a flaky connect recovers instead of hanging. Then the bells and whistles: **16-bit color at 80 MHz SPI** on the S3, and the **radar sweep with a comet trail paced at 30 fps**. By the end it was a live scope — round LCD, green grid, real callsigns — sitting in the printed slatted cube on the desk.

recent.title: Disco-ball satellite — and a nasty ground-noise lesson

media.caption: Printed skull over the spinning disco ball

recent.body: Added a motorized disco ball as its own satellite (stepper + spot LED + OLED) with a dedicated LiveTarget. First version ran the stepper off main power and it made the ground filthy — the noise bled into the rest of the Noodle. Its own supply fixed it. Classic motor-on-shared-ground trap.

recent.title: Audio-reactive ambient effects + kaleidoscope pass
recent.body: Made all 16 ambient effects audio-reactive — first the ambient set and a base-LED audio mode, then mappings for the remaining 12, then a punch-up on Plasma/Galaxy/Stripes/Puzzle with a base-LED audio overlay. Added a kaleidoscope post-processing pass on top of the ambient effects and a drama slider to dial the intensity.

recent.title: vizBot 3.0 — StackChan body target
recent.body: vizBot 3.0 put the face on a StackChan body. Built up in phases: a minimum-viable StackChan build target, StackChan hardware driver bring-up, web endpoints with pitch safety clamping, then servo expressivity, touch reactions, idle sweeps, and a chill mode. Replaced the old ambient effects with 16 patterns ported from noodle-v2. Had to pin M5GFX@0.2.19 — 0.2.21 gave the Core S3 a black screen.

recent.title: ESP-NOW only, plus a screen-capture path

media.caption: Lit desk with the pixel matrix running

recent.body: Dropped WiFi association entirely — the Console runs pure ESP-NOW now. Started the screen-share path (browser → ingest → matrix) and a LittleFS clip store, so I can push real captured pixels to the 16×16, not just generated effects.

recent.title: Dial remote, sprite overlays, playlists

media.caption: Hex panels and RGB orb on the bench

recent.body: Added the dial sat as a wireless remote with a live preview canvas, a composite overlay source (16×16 pattern + centered 8×8 icon), Qwiic forward/back buttons for the pattern stack, and curated playlists. Also cut the dead DDP path entirely.

recent.title: The fleet takes shape — bar, 8×8, 16×16 satellites
recent.body: Built out the pixel satellites — a 1×30 bar, an 8×8 icon panel, a 16×16 matrix — each its own board rendering locally off a shared wire format (v5). The GPIO wall is officially gone; I scale by adding boards now.

recent.title: Audio satellite — first ESP-NOW peer, beat detection
recent.body: First satellite: a separate board with a mic running spectral-flux, bass-leaning beat detection, broadcasting audio features over peered ESP-NOW so every effect can react in lockstep. This is where it stopped being one board.

recent.title: Three encoders, per-target ownership, Source Map
recent.body: Wired up three NeoPixel rotary encoders with per-target slot ownership (highest I2C address = slot 0), a Source Map for per-surface assignment, and retired Pixelblaze in favor of the native engine. The control surface is starting to feel like a real instrument panel.

recent.title: Descriptor-table effect engine + the FeatherWing

media.caption: The full instrument lit

recent.body: Stood up the real effects engine — a descriptor table, 10 effects to start — plus a 4×8 NeoPixel FeatherWing mirroring the matrix and a TPS61169 gamma-corrected filament driver. The whole surface is lit and animating together now.

recent.title: Ran out of pins — going distributed
recent.body: Added an external 8×8 and hit the GPIO wall. That's the decision point: every LED surface becomes its own ESP-NOW satellite, so the system scales by adding boards, not pins. Everything after this is that idea playing out.

recent.title: Filaments breathing, fiber optics, live Pixelblaze

media.caption: Driver board lighting fiber-optic strands

recent.body: PCA9685 LED filaments on a sine-breath offset, a Pixelblaze websocket path for browsing and streaming patterns live, and the patterns/ scaffolding. First time the thing looked less like a prototype and more like an instrument.

recent.title: Dual-core FreeRTOS — network off the render path
recent.body: Decomposed the firmware into four FreeRTOS tasks across both cores, moving the network onto Core 0 so the radio and the LED render stop fighting each other. This is the backbone everything else hangs off.

recent.title: Noodle 2.0 — core up and running in a day
recent.body: Rebuilt from the breadboard onto a FeatherS3. In one sitting: display + encoder + buttons working, a sensor dashboard (distance, light, NeoPixel), WLED control, and a direct 4×12 matrix with an 8×8 icon slideshow. The solid STEMMA-QT prototyping paid off immediately.

recent.title: PlatformIO migration + a SAM2695 MIDI synth
recent.body: Moved vizbot and vizpow off the Arduino IDE onto PlatformIO for reproducible builds and versioned firmware binaries, with bins published to a top-level builds/ directory. Integrated a SAM2695 MIDI synthesizer across several phases, including cloud MIDI sequence caching and sync so the bot can pull tunes down. It plays MIDI now in addition to speech.

recent.title: Import upcoming shows into a tour, modular admin routes
recent.body:
Added an admin feature to import upcoming shows straight into a tour, so setting up a new
season is a few clicks instead of hand-entering a schedule. This came after splitting the
admin routes out of one giant file into modular pieces — the console had grown enough that
the routing needed to be maintainable, not just working. The refactor keeps the cost of
adding the next feature down.

recent.title: Noodle 1 — the breadboard prototype that didn't scale
recent.body:
First pass at the idea: one controller driving a series of LED grids and
filaments. Built it on a breadboard with a rat's nest of wires. It worked, barely,
but it was obvious this would never scale — every new surface meant more jumpers
and more flakiness. Tore it down and went looking for a more solid way to
prototype (landed on Adafruit STEMMA QT modules).

recent.title: vizCloud, multi-bot orchestration, and an ESP-NOW mesh
recent.body: Landed vizCloud integration with a static BSS framebuffer for zero-flicker TLS, an isolated cloud task on Core 0, and a unified WiFi task. Built Stage 4/5 multi-bot orchestration on top of it. Added an ESP-NOW local mesh doing cooperative WLED arbitration — flag bits in a broadcast packet so two bots won't drive the same matrix at once, with one deferring its speech bubble until a peer releases the display.

recent.title: Senses — mic, proximity, light, and a hologram mode
recent.body: Added sensor input: a mic audio-analysis driver, a proximity + ambient-light sensor driver, sound-reactive and proximity-reactive expressions, and auto-brightness. Reworked the face with 6 eye shapes, 6 mouth shapes, and 8 new expressions, and redid the speech bubble with a proportional font that positions off the sensors. Added a hologram mode — a horizontal LCD mirror for a Pepper's-ghost prism.

recent.title: LovyanGFX migration + a tween system
recent.body: Migrated the LCD target from Arduino_GFX to LovyanGFX; chased a blue tint and dim brightness afterward, and unified canvas management along the way. Built a tween system with 8 easing functions and wired it into the main loop, replacing the hand-rolled smoothstep and linear lerps. Expression transitions and look-around animations now run on the easing curves.

recent.title: M5 Core S3 target + per-device identity
recent.body: Added an M5Stack Core S3 target with a multi-screen layout system: a layout.h that derives the UI from screen size, so a new display is a compile flag rather than a rewrite. Gave each bot its own identity — a unique per-device SSID and mDNS hostname derived from the eFuse MAC, plus a user-settable device name for a memorable hostname. Groundwork for running more than one bot at a time.

recent.title: WLED integration — from scroll effects to raw DDP
recent.body: Added forwarding of the bot's speech to a WLED LED matrix. First approach drove WLED's built-in scrolling text effect; fought it for days over scroll speed, trails, jump cuts, and effect reinit on consecutive words. Switched to direct pixel control over DDP, drawing the text myself, which gave immediate clean frames without relying on the effect engine.

recent.title: Networking hardening and the Core 0 crash
recent.body: Spent several days hardening the networking. Added a sequential boot loader with onscreen diagnostics, an I2C mutex and command queue for race safety, moved the web server to a FreeRTOS task on Core 0, added WiFi provisioning with NVS-stored credentials, and a captive portal with DNS + mDNS auto-redirect. The Core 0 crash took the longest — chased it through watchdog reconfigures and stack-size bumps before the WiFi task stayed up. Closed out with persistent settings and a health heartbeat.

recent.title: Face engine and the split into vizBot
recent.body: Built the face engine in phases: core face with 12 expressions, then sayings and speech bubbles, then personality presets and a full web UI, then 20 expressions with backgrounds. Everything is drawn from primitives so it scales with the screen. Split the firmware in two — vizpow keeps the effects, vizbot gets the face — and renamed the WiFi AP from VizPow to vizBot.

recent.title: Hi-res LCD, an ESP8266 port, and the vizPow name
recent.body: Brought up a hi-res LCD rendering mode with a touch menu so the effects render on a real screen, not just a matrix. Ported the engine to an ESP8266 LED matrix target to test how portable it was. Renamed the project to vizPow. Same core engine, more display surfaces.

recent.title: Emoji mode, icon sprites, and shake-to-switch
recent.body: Added an emoji display mode with a sprite picker and 32 icon sprites, plus icon tooling to manage them. Wired up a shuffle-bag auto-cycle for effects and palettes so they don't repeat too soon. Added a shake gesture read off the IMU to change modes.

recent.title: Bring-up — ESP32-S3 LED matrix controller
recent.body: Started the project as a plain ESP32-S3 LED matrix controller. Sorted the build config, laid out the folder structure, and pushed pixels to the grid. Scope at this point is a board, a matrix, and a controller that renders effects — no face, no cloud, no gestures yet.

recent.title: Tour Wrapped recap page and personalized email links
recent.body:
Built a Tour Wrapped stats page: a per-player recap of the tour just played — your best
calls, your points, your rarities. Wired a personalized wrappedLink variable into the email
system so every player gets a direct link to their own recap, keyed to the right tour. It
took a few follow-up fixes to make the callout point at the correct completed tour, and
Wrapped turned out to be the thing people actually shared.

recent.title: Final summer-tour data pull, season closeout
recent.body:
Ran the last data pull for summer tour and let the season settle. The cycle for running
this: a burst of live scoring while shows are happening, then a quiet stretch to reconcile
data, fix what scored wrong, and get ready for the next run. First full tour season in the
books.

recent.title: Scores dashboard and a stats sidebar
recent.body:
Shipped a scores dashboard and a stats sidebar alongside the research tools: a song
explorer with a selector, tour-plays columns, and the numbers players use to reason about
what the band will open with. The research side is where the hardcore players build
predictions off gap data and tour history rather than guesses.

recent.title: Live mode: scoring as the show happens
recent.body:
Summer tour meant live mode: a live view that scores predictions in near real time as a
setlist comes in, with an admin side to drive it song by song. Added a compact setlist
display for the live page and pushed bustout callouts right into it, so the leaderboard
reshuffles as each song is entered while the band is still playing.

recent.title: Tour manager and per-tour song counts
recent.body:
Built a tour manager and started tracking per-tour song counts — how many times each song
has been played on the current run. Phish is organized by tour, so almost every view worth
having — leaderboards, research, Wrapped stats — depends on knowing which shows belong to
which tour. Getting that structure right unlocked a lot of the features that came after.

recent.title: Email manager 1.0
recent.body:
Stood up the transactional email system on Resend: a composer, refined templates, and a
logs viewer to see what actually went out. The old ad-hoc emailers are gone, replaced by
one manager driven from the admin side. A day later I added a rate limiter so a large send
can't get the domain flagged.

recent.title: Editing setlists by hand
recent.body:
Added an admin interface for editing setlist details directly, because the official data
isn't always right, or isn't posted yet, and the whole scoring run depends on it. Now a
mangled setlist can be corrected or an auto-generated one refined before it scores, with
better error handling for when the source data is malformed. The scoring run is only as
good as the setlist it's fed.

recent.title: Admin console 1.0
recent.body:
Built the back office: admin pages to manage files, songs, users, and WookBot setlists
from one place. Running a live game means constantly touching data — fixing a song entry,
checking an account, curating a generated setlist — and doing that directly against the
database was getting slow. The console replaced a batch of one-off scripts with actual
screens.

recent.title: Scoring engine: bustout detection from gap data, bonus breakdown
recent.body:
Reworked the scoring engine for fairness. Bustout detection now uses gap data — the stretch
of shows since a song was last played — so calling a rarity is worth real bonus points, and
shared bustouts pay out to everyone who called them. Tightened the exact-position accuracy
scoring, and started surfacing the bonus breakdown on the score page so players can see
exactly why they earned each point instead of trusting a single total.

recent.title: WookBot: OpenAI setlist generator goes public
recent.body:
WookBot went public: an OpenAI-backed generator that drafts a plausible setlist for an
upcoming show from historical play patterns. Gave it a home-page module showing the show
date and venue, a selector to browse past generations, and skeleton loading states during
generation. It only pulls from published show data, so the suggestions stay grounded in
songs the band actually plays.

recent.title: Leaderboards: global, tour, single-show
recent.body:
Added leaderboards with three scopes: a global board across all players, a per-tour board
scoped to the current run, and a single-show board for one show's predictions. Each board
ranks the top predictors for its scope, and each board's view buttons link straight to the
relevant scorecards, so you can go from a ranked name to that player's scored prediction in
one click. This is the piece that turns scored predictions into an ongoing competition
between shows.

recent.title: Random-fill button, setlist-save fixes, spam-folder reminder
recent.body:
Closing out the first playable week. Added a random-fill button that populates a setlist
with random songs, for people who want to jump in without building one by hand. Fixed a
batch of setlist-saving bugs that had been dropping songs. Added a check-your-spam-folder
reminder for the account verification email, since sign-ups were coming in and the
verification mail was landing in spam folders.

recent.title: Scorecards and the first scored show
recent.body:
Built the scorecard: a two-column set 1 / set 2 layout with a breakdown showing which
songs contributed to your points. Wired in real 2024 show data to score predictions
against, so a finished prediction could be scored for the first time. The score button
stays hidden until a show is officially scored, so players don't see a wall of zeros
before the band has played.

recent.title: First commit: build-a-setlist UI, song database, prediction saving
recent.body:
First commit. The build-a-setlist UI is on screen: drop songs into slots, reorder them,
and add sets as you go. Seeded the song database by pulling from several phish.net
endpoints, then cached the result to a local JSON file so the game doesn't hit the API on
every load. Prediction saving landed the same day, so the core loop — build a setlist,
save it as a prediction — was working end to end from day one.
